title.rendered: Scripting the Experience: My Evolution from Filmmaker to Product Designer

content.rendered:
Two years ago, my “users” were audiences in a darkened theater. As a film director and screenwriter, I spent my career obsessing over narrative arcs, emotional resonance, and the “why” behind every scene.

Transitioning into Product Design through my Master’s at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) wasn’t a pivot away from storytelling it was an evolution of it. Product designers are essentially directors for digital stages. To build impactful products, you need more than just aesthetic skills; you need to understand the human psyche, the strategic constraints of AI, and the underlying logic of code.

Here is how three pivotal courses at CMU refined my toolkit to build for the next generation of tech products. (1. Designing for AI products and Services, 2. Persuasive Design, 3. Fundamentals of Programming and Computer Sciences 15-112)

1. Designing for AI: Managing the “Unpredictable Actor”

The Skill: Bridging the gap between technical feasibility and human value.

In film, you often work with “unpredictable” elements, lighting, weather, or an actor’s improvisation. AI is the ultimate unpredictable actor. In my course work for CMU HCII’s course Designing for AI Services and Products taught by industry veterans Dan Saffer and Leon Zhang, I stopped viewing AI as “magic” and started viewing it as a design tool.

For my final project, our team utilized a Matchmaking framework to identify exactly where AI capabilities, such as NLP and predictive modeling, could solve real-world friction.

  • The Strategic Edge: The challenge in modern design isn’t just making a feature; it’s ensuring it is helpful even when the model “hallucinates.” In the HORSE project, we didn’t just design a dashboard; we designed a Value Flow that transformed a $13M annual loss into a $2M annual saving. By utilizing Agentic AI to automate competitive bidding and internal resource allocation, we reduced the time spent on manual scheduling by over 40 hours per cycle, allowing staff to focus on patient care rather than logistics.

Project Spotlight: HORSE: Agentic AI for Hospital Staffing

The Vision: Moving hospital staffing from reactive firefighting to proactive, autonomous optimization.

The Problem: The $13M Staffing Crisis

Current hospital staffing is rigid and manual, requiring roughly 13.4 hours to build a single four-week schedule and an additional 40.3 hours to fix avoidable issues. This inefficiency leads to a dependency on “premium labor,” costing hospitals between $10M and $13.5M annually for travel nurses alone.

The Solution: An Autonomous Staffing Agent

HORSE is an AI-driven platform that autonomously generates routine schedules while dynamically adjusting to real-time changes. The project demonstrates three core AI “Matchmaking” capabilities:

  • Real-Time Adaptability: The agent tracks live changes in patient intake and staff shortages to adjust coverage immediately.
  • Predictive Forecasting: By analyzing past patient data (e.g., severe winter surges), the model forecasts future staffing gaps before they occur.
  • Automated Execution & Bidding: When a gap is identified, the agent prioritizes the lowest-cost internal float nurses first (saving 45% vs. market rates) before directly executing competitive bidding for external travel nurses.

Strategic & Financial Impact

This project wasn’t just a technical exercise; it was a lesson in Financial Feasibility.

  • Annual Savings: We projected annual returns of $1.6M to $2.65M per hospital through reductions in travel nurse reliance and overtime cuts.
  • Technical Feasibility: We mapped the integration of real-time data (HL7/FHIR APIs) with optimization solvers (OR-Tools, Gurobi) to ensure the agent operated within strict staffing constraints.
HORSEDownload

2. Persuasive Design: Engineering Fairness through Psychology

The Skill: Using psychological frameworks to build digital products fostering positive social change.

In CMU HCII’s Persuasive Design course taught by prolific HCI researcher Dr. Geoff Kaufman, I moved from narrative intuition to scientific intervention.

Our project, Peeriodic, was a (dating app style) team-formation app designed to interrupt unconscious gender bias in the college STEM group project experience. We applied two core psychological concepts to the UI:

  • System 1 thinking(Fast/Intuitive): We used a timed blind swiping mechanism to capture initial instincts but obfuscated identifying factors (names, photos) of the possible groupmates to prevent snap-judgment bias.
  • System 2 thinking(Slow/Deliberate): We triggered Hypocrisy Induction. When a user discovered their “ideal teammate” was someone they might have stereotyped, it forced a moment of reflection and cognitive dissonance reduction.
  • The Impact: By moving a Self-Affirmation module to the start of the user flow, we primed underrepresented users with confidence.
  • Here’s a figma prototype of our final product.
05315_BiasBustersDownload

3. 15-112: Technical Empathy for the Builders

The Skill: Algorithmic thinking and cross-functional leadership.

To lead a partnership with engineers, a designer must speak their language. 15-112: Fundamentals of Programming is famously the most rigorous course at CMU.

I didn’t just learn to code. By learning top-down design in Python from scratch, handling recursion, object-oriented programming, and efficiency, I gained a deep respect for the “how” behind the “what.”

  • The Collaborative Edge: Designers don’t work in a vacuum. My technical background means I can sit in a room with engineers and understand the computational cost of a design choice.

The “Director’s Cut” on Product Design

A film director leads a crew of 30+ to turn a script into a tangible reality. A Product Designer leads a cross-functional team to turn a conceptual idea into a global tool.

My journey from the set to the screen has given me a unique edge: the ability to see the Big Picture (Strategy), understand the Subtext (Psychology), and a foundational grasp on the Technical Craft (Code). I am no longer just telling stories; I am building the platforms where the world tells theirs.

title.rendered: CMU Datascience Club + Introduction to Applied Machine Learning + Datathon 2026

content.rendered:
My journey into the world of data at Carnegie Mellon has been a strenuous climb, starting with the fundamentals of machine learning theory, moving through deep learning frameworks, and finally deploying AI agents to tackle UN global humanitarian datasets. Here is the story of how I built my toolkit.

The Starting Point: Applied Machine Learning & NLP

From Fundamentals to Frontiers: My Data Science Journey at CMU

My journey into the world of data at Carnegie Mellon has been a rigorous climb, starting with the theoretical foundations of machine learning, moving through deep learning frameworks, and finally deploying AI agents to solve global humanitarian crises. Here is how I built my toolkit.

1. The Foundation: Applied Machine Learning (17-634)

The journey began in CMU’s Applied Machine Learning course, which serves as a broad survey of supervised and unsupervised methods. This course is designed to bridge the gap between theoretical assumptions and practical application in data processing pipelines. Key topics covered in the curriculum include:

  • Core Concepts: Random variables, Bayes Rule, MLE, and MAP.
  • Classifiers: Deep dives into Generative and Discriminative classifiers like Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression.
  • Advanced Modeling: Support Vector Machines (SVM), Kernel methods, and ensemble techniques like Bagging and Boosting.
  • NLP & Evaluation: Topic modeling (LDA), error analysis, and fairness in statistical models.

For my final research paper in this course, I applied these principles to Natural Language Processing (NLP), specifically multi-class emotion detection. Using the dair-ai/emotion dataset, I classified text into six emotional states: sadness, joy, love, anger, fear, and surprise.

  • Tooling: I utilized Weka and LightSide to reproduce preprocessing steps and ensure experimental consistency.
  • Modeling: I established a baseline using SVM classifiers and Bag-of-Words features.
  • Refinement: Through rigorous error analysis and tuning the SVM complexity parameters, I learned how regularization can significantly improve generalization in high-dimensional text data.

My final paper can be found here:

Applied ML final paper_Samantha LaiDownload

Expanding the Toolkit: PyTorch and Computer Vision

With a grasp of classical ML, I joined the CMU Data Science Club to tackle the frontier of Deep Learning. At the September 2025 PyTorch Workshop, I shifted my focus from text to pixels.

Participating in the CMU Data Science Club has been an transformative experience, evolving from a standard academic activity to the launchpad for impactful data-driven innovation. My journey this year, culminating in the CMU 2026 Datathon, perfect exemplifies this progression. Here’s a look back at how I went from attending introductory workshops to submitting a project utilizing advanced AI agents on the Databricks platform.

The Foundation: Deep Learning with PyTorch

The core project at the workshop was both practical and challenging: Road Signage Prediction. We worked on developing models to predict road signs (Crosswalk, Speed Limit, Stop, Traffic Light) from a complex dataset of 4-channel (RGBA) images at 256×256 resolution. This wasn’t just theoretical, we tackled real-world hurdles like handling unbalanced datasets and optimizing training using GPU acceleration (CUDA) in Google Colab.

This workshop didn’t just teach syntax; it provided a deep dive into neural network architectures, from fundamental logic to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Learning about advanced training techniques like Dropout, BatchNorm, Weight Decay, and utilizing advanced optimizers like Adam, gave me the tools necessary for building models that generalize well. It also introduced me to powerful tracking tools like Weights & Biases (W&B).

  • Sample boilerplate training loop visualized during our workshop.

Key Takeaway from this phase: “A winning model is rarely the first one you train. The real power is in the ability to iterate quickly and rigorously track experiment results.”

The Challenge: The CMU 2026 Datathon

Equipped with this technical expertise, I eagerly joined the CMU 2026 Datathon. The datathon, sponsored by Databricks and the UN, presented a perfect arena to apply these skills but also demanded something more: the ability to tackle sophisticated, messy, and large-scale data to drive meaningful insights.

I decided to tackle a globally relevant and humanitarian issue, one of the two topics/datasets the UN provided for the datathon. My goal was not just to analyze numbers, but to create a model that identifies, “Forgotten Crises” countries, where the human need significantly outstrips financial resources and international aid.

The Innovation: AI Agents and Databricks

The defining aspect of our approach was the integration of cutting-edge technology. Datathons require rapid innovation, and we found our accelerant in AI Agents within the Databricks platform.

My project required merging disparate, complex global datasets, including:

  1. Humanitarian Response Plans (HRP) for financial data.
  2. Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) for ‘People in Need’ (PIN) metrics.
  3. Vulnerable Population Statistics specifically looking at the child population (ages 0-17).

Using AI agents on Databricks provided a game-changing advantage. The agents helped automate several critical steps:

  • Intelligent Data Mapping: The agents helped manage the complex task of joining global datasets with varying country naming conventions and different reporting cycles.
  • Automated Feature Engineering: They identified meaningful relationships, allowing us to rapidly develop a normalized “Neglect Index.” This index prioritized countries by the widest gaps in USD-per-person-in-need.
  • Predictive Modeling Automation: While I provided the domain direction, the agents accelerated the development of our time-series models, predicting neglected crises for the years 2024 through 2026.

The Result: Insight that Matters

The culmination of my work was the Geo-Insight Analysis submission. By analyzing 24 countries across three years, my model definitively highlighted the crises receiving the lowest USD per person in need.

My analysis identified Myanmar, Colombia, Venezuela, Afghanistan, and Sudan as the most underfunded humanitarian crises by 2026. This went beyond data science, it was social impact analytics, designed to help organizations better understand where intervention is needed most.

Furthermore, I utilized Databricks and Redash to build dynamic, interactive visualizations (including choropleth maps) that instantly localized funding discrepancies and made the “Forgotten Crises” visible.

Here is my final submisson:

Geo_Insight_Analysis_UpdatedDownload

Conclusion: Continuous Evolution

Looking back, the trajectory is clear: the CMU Data Science Club’s PyTorch workshop provided the technical literacy. The CMU Datathon provided the venue and challenge. But integrating AI agents via Databricks allowed us to leap from simple prediction to a scalable, automated analytical solution with real-world humanitarian application.

My journey this year is a testament to the club’s mission, not just to teach code, but to foster the critical thinking and tool proficiency that allows students to tackle the most complex challenges of our time.

During my time in Carnegie Mellon University’s Entertainment Technology Center (ETC), I participated in the signature Building Virtual Worlds (BVW) course, founded by Randy Pausch. BVW is a hands-on, interdisciplinary, project-based course that challenges students to design and build immersive interactive experiences within tight deadlines, often in intensive two-week sprints. The course emphasizes collaboration across artistic, technical, and narrative disciplines, pushing students to iterate rapidly while presenting their work publicly in showcases attended by peers, faculty, and industry guests.

In BVW, I contributed to four rapid prototyping projects:

Christmas Mission – Producer, Designer, Sound Designer

Co-produced and designed the soundscape for a 4-player networked fog-of-war strategy game where player communication was central. Developed the thematic concept, guided multiplayer UX design, coordinated team meetings, and structured playtests to gather feedback and meet iterative design goals on schedule.

EyeSpy – Designer, Sound Designer, Narrative Lead

Proposed integrating Tobii Eye Tracker hardware for innovative Pictionary-style gameplay. Designed and directed live-action cutscenes, writing dialogue and guiding actors to enhance narrative immersion. Successfully validated a non-traditional input method for interactive play.

Soultown Taxi – Producer, Designer, Narrative Lead

Led a diverse team through a two-week rapid production cycle to develop a Meta Quest 3 VR game, creating narrative dialogue for a ghost client and designing gameplay mechanics, ensuring a cohesive story within strict platform constraints.

Cat Meow Spa – Producer, Designer, Narrative Lead

Developed a game using the Microsoft Adaptive Controller, focusing on accessibility and intuitive interactions for players managing a conveyor belt system. Directed cutscenes and drafted storyboards, demonstrating adaptability in inclusive game design.

Through BVW, I honed skills in rapid prototyping, interdisciplinary collaboration, iterative design, and accessible interactive storytelling, reflecting the ETC’s signature approach to hands-on, industry-focused entertainment technology education.
